summaries.example: Imagine a jar with red, blue, and yellow marbles. You know that 30 of 90 marbles are red, but you do not know how many of the others are blue or yellow. You may feel sure that red has a one-third chance, while the chances of blue and yellow could be many different numbers. An imprecise model keeps this uncertainty instead of forcing you to choose one exact number.
summaries.summary: Probability helps us describe uncertainty. The usual approach asks for one exact probability, such as 0.5. But sometimes our evidence does not justify that much exactness. Imprecise probabilities use several possible probabilities instead of one. This can show that we are unsure about the evidence, that different people disagree, or that we are suspending judgment. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry explains why philosophers and researchers use this idea, how it can be represented with a set of probability functions, and what puzzles it creates. For example, learning something can sometimes make the range of possible beliefs wider, and complete ignorance can make it difficult to learn from new evidence. The entry presents these arguments and problems as topics of continuing discussion.
key_ideas: Ordinary probability models often use one exact number for each belief.
Imprecise probability models can use a set or interval of possible numbers.
This approach can represent uncertainty, disagreement, and choosing not to decide yet.
The approach also raises questions about how beliefs should change after learning and how choices should be made.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make decisions with incomplete information. Pretending to know an exact chance can give a misleading picture of what the evidence supports. Imprecise probabilities offer a way to keep uncertainty visible, while also reminding us that a useful model must explain learning, reasoning, and choice.

important_terms.definition: A way to describe how likely something is when the evidence does not support one exact number.
A number, such as 1/2, used to show how strongly someone believes an event will happen.
Not knowing which of several possible chances is correct, even when the possibilities are clearly described.
A collection of possible probability rules used together to represent one set of beliefs.

questions_to_think_about: Is not knowing the exact chance different from believing the chance is exactly one-half?
When might it be sensible to refuse a bet because the evidence is too weak?
Can a group with disagreeing members have one fair probability?
Should new information always make us more confident?

summaries.example: Return to the Ellsberg urn: 90 marbles include 30 red ones, while the remaining 60 are blue or yellow in an unknown mixture. A person may prefer betting on red rather than blue because red has a known chance but blue has an unknown chance. Yet that person may also prefer betting on “not red” rather than “not blue,” reversing the comparison when the ambiguity changes sides. A single precise probability function cannot represent this preference pattern, whereas a set of probability functions can represent a fixed one-third probability for red and a range of possibilities for blue and yellow. The source notes that this is one motivation for imprecise probability, though alternative explanations
summaries.summary: Imprecise probabilities are models of belief that relax the orthodox requirement that every proposition receive one exact numerical probability. Instead, a belief state may be represented by a set of probability functions, called a credal set or representor. The resulting lower and upper envelopes give bounds, but the full set contains more information than those bounds alone. The approach is motivated by several kinds of uncertainty: ambiguity, incomplete or conflicting evidence, unknown correlations, suspension of judgment, possible nonprobabilistic chances, and disagreement among members of a group. The Ellsberg case illustrates why someone might favor known risk over unknown ambiguity, even when no single precise probability can rationalize the resulting choices. Other arguments concern incomparability, the distinction between the weight and balance of evidence, and the ability to avoid betting when evidence is silent. The entry also examines serious problems. Dilation occurs when updating widens a probability range; vacuous priors can produce belief inertia; and decision rules may struggle when the credal set supports conflicting actions. Further issues concern what credences represent, why a set of probabilities should be the right stopping point rather than a set of sets, and how imprecise beliefs should be scored. The overall conclusion is not that IP has decisively replaced precise probabilism, but that it offers a promising way to model severe uncertainty while leaving important questions open.
key_ideas: Imprecise probability replaces a single probability function with a set of such functions, often summarized by lower and upper bounds.
Its motivations include ambiguity aversion, incomplete or conflicting evidence, unknown relationships between events, suspension of judgment, nonstandard chances, and disagreement within groups.
Indifference is not the same as incomparability: equal preference says two options are equally good, while incomparability withholds a ranking.
The interval for one proposition is not the whole belief state; relationships among propositions can be lost if we record only separate ranges.
IP faces challenges involving dilation, belief inertia, sequential decision-making, interpretation, regress, and standards for accuracy.
The source presents precise probabilism as a useful ideal or model in some settings, while treating the advantages and limits of IP as unsettled philosophical questions.
summaries.why_it_matters: A probability model is not only a calculation device; it can also be a theory of rational belief. If evidence is incomplete or ambiguous, a single number may suggest more determination than the evidence warrants. IP can preserve that lack of determination and represent disagreement. At the same time, its complications show that a theory of belief must explain how information changes belief, how beliefs guide action, and what makes one representation better than another.

important_terms.definition: The standard view that a rational belief state is represented by one probability function assigning a real number to every proposition.
A model that represents belief with a set of probability functions rather than one function.
A set of probability functions used to represent the possible opinions making up a belief state.
A lower bound on the probabilities assigned to a proposition by members of a credal set.
An upper bound on the probabilities assigned to a proposition by members of a credal set.
Uncertainty about outcomes whose possible probabilities are unknown or only partly known, unlike risk with known probabilities.
A state in which evidence does not settle on a particular belief or ranking, without thereby saying that the options are equally good.
A case in which updating produces a wider range of probabilities than the original range.

questions_to_think_about: Does a rational agent need to assign one exact probability to every proposition?
Is refusing to rank two options different from judging them equally good?
If a model represents ignorance with the full interval from 0 to 1, can it update effectively?
Does dilation show a defect in imprecise probability, or a feature of representing unresolved possibilities?
What should count as a good or accurate imprecise belief?

summaries.example: Suppose a school club is planning an outdoor event. The weather forecast gives no useful information about rain. A precise approach might require assigning one number, such as a 50% chance of rain. But the club may reasonably say that the evidence does not support any particular number. An imprecise approach could keep many possible chances in view. If two members disagree about the forecast, the same set of probabilities might also represent their unresolved disagreement. The group could then avoid treating a guess as settled fact.
summaries.summary: The entry compares two ways of representing belief under uncertainty. Precise probability assigns one exact number to each proposition. Imprecise probability instead uses a collection of probability functions, often summarized by lower and upper limits. This can express the thought that evidence is incomplete, conflicted, or too ambiguous to support one exact answer. It can also represent a group whose members disagree without pretending that they have reached a single consensus. One important example is the Ellsberg problem. People may prefer a bet with a known chance to one whose chance is unknown, even when a single precise model cannot explain all their choices. Supporters of IP also emphasize the difference between indifference and incomparability, and between the amount of evidence and which side the evidence favors. The theory is not without problems. Dilation can make a belief range expand after learning. A completely open prior may fail to narrow when evidence arrives, a problem called belief inertia. Decision-making is also difficult when different probability functions recommend different actions. The source discusses competing interpretations and responses rather than presenting these disputes as settled. It concludes that IP is a useful family of models for severe uncertainty, but that its formal and philosophical foundations still need further work.
key_ideas: Precise probabilities are powerful, but they can impose more exactness than our evidence deserves.
Imprecise probabilities can represent ambiguity, ignorance, conflicting evidence, and disagreement among people.
The Ellsberg problem suggests that people may prefer known risk to unknown ambiguity, a pattern a single probability may not explain.
A range of probabilities is only a summary; the full relationships among the possible probability functions can matter.
Imprecise models may create difficulties: learning can widen beliefs, very broad starting beliefs may resist learning, and choices may become hard to compare.
Philosophers disagree about whether imprecision is required, merely allowed, or mainly useful as a description of actual reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: In science, public policy, and everyday planning, evidence is often incomplete. A model that forces one exact number may hide uncertainty or disagreement. Imprecise probabilities give thinkers another way to describe what the evidence supports. Studying their weaknesses is equally important because a good model should help us learn and decide, not merely display uncertainty.

important_terms.definition: The usual probability approach, in which each proposition receives one exact numerical probability.
An approach that represents a belief with multiple possible probabilities rather than one exact value.
A set of probability functions that together represent an agent’s or group’s possible beliefs.
A situation in which the outcomes are uncertain and their probabilities are known or specified.
A situation in which the outcomes’ probabilities are unknown or only partly known.
Having no preference between two choices because they seem equally good, rather than because they cannot be fairly compared.
Having no settled ranking between choices; this is different from deciding that they are equally good.

questions_to_think_about: Would a 50% forecast always mean the same thing as having no useful evidence?
Why might someone prefer a known risk to an unknown chance?
Is being undecided the same as thinking two choices are equally good?
When does keeping many possibilities open help, and when might it prevent learning?
Should a model of a group’s belief preserve disagreement among its members?
